title: Scope, Lifetime and Namespaces
summary: **Scope** is *where in the code* a name can be used. **Lifetime** is *when during the run* the variable exists. **Namespaces** group names so that two things called the same do not clash.
markdown:
## Two questions about every variable | Question | Called | Decided | |---|---|---| | On which lines may I use this name? | **Scope** | By where it is declared in the source | | For how long does the value exist in memory? | **Lifetime** | While the program runs | For the local variables you have used so far the two coincide, which is why they are easy to mix up. They come apart in the next lesson. ## Every pair of braces is a scope A name declared inside a block can be used from its declaration to the block's closing brace. ``` ┌─ main ───────────────────────────────────┐ │ int x{ 1 }; │ │ │ │ ┌─ if block ─────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ int y{ 2 }; │ │ │ │ can use: x, y │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ ┌─ for block ──────────────────┐ │ │ │ │ │ int z{ 3 }; │ │ │ │ │ │ can use: x, y, z │ │ │ │ │ └──────────────────────────────┘ │ │ │ │ z is out of scope │ │ │ └────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │ y and z are out of scope │ └──────────────────────────────────────────┘ ``` **Code can see outwards, never inwards.** An inner block can use names from the blocks around it. An outer block cannot reach into an inner one. ## Lifetime of a local variable ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant Code participant Memory Code->>Memory: execution reaches int y{ 2 } Note over Memory: y exists Code->>Memory: execution reaches the closing brace Note over Memory: y is destroyed ``` A local variable is created when execution reaches its definition and destroyed at the closing brace of its block. That is automatic, and it explains the name for this kind of lifetime: **automatic storage duration**. > [!tip] Keep scopes small > Declare each variable in the smallest block that needs it, as close to its first use as you can. Fewer lines can touch it, so fewer lines can break it. ## Shadowing An inner block may declare a name that already exists in an outer block. The inner one **hides** the outer one until its block ends. ```cpp #include int main() { int apples{ 5 }; { int apples{ 10 }; // a second, separate variable std::cout << apples << '\n'; // 10 } std::cout << apples << '\n'; // 5 return 0; } ``` This is legal and almost always a mistake. You think you are changing one variable and you are changing another. Give the inner variable a different name. ## Namespaces As programs grow, names collide. Two libraries may each have a function called `add`. A **namespace** is a named group that keeps them apart, in the way a surname separates two people called Sam. ```mermaid flowchart TD G["the global namespace"] --> STD["std
cout, string, ..."] G --> M["Math
add, pi"] G --> GA["Game
add, Player"] GA --> GAU["Game::Utils
clamp"] ``` ```cpp #include namespace Math { constexpr double pi{ 3.14159 }; int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } } namespace Game::Utils { int clamp(int value, int low, int high) { return value < low ? low : (value > high ? high : value); } } int main() { std::cout << Math::add(2, 3) << ' ' << Math::pi << '\n'; std::cout << Game::Utils::clamp(15, 0, 10) << '\n'; // 10 return 0; } ``` `::` is the **scope resolution operator**. Read `Math::add` as "the `add` that lives in `Math`". You have used it since your first program: `std::cout` is "the `cout` in `std`". A name declared outside every function and every namespace belongs to the **global namespace**. ## `using`: shorter names, with a cost | Form | Effect | Verdict | |---|---|---| | `using std::cout;` | Lets you write `cout` for this one name | Fine inside a function or a `.cpp` file | | `using namespace std;` | Brings in **every** name from `std` | Avoid | | `namespace GU = Game::Utils;` | A short alias for a long namespace | Fine | > [!danger] Why this course never writes `using namespace std;` > `std` contains thousands of names, including common words such as `count`, `max`, `distance` and `swap`. Importing all of them invites clashes with your own names, and the errors that result are baffling. In a **header** it is worse still, because it leaks into every file that includes that header. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What is the difference between scope and lifetime? - They mean the same thing + Scope is where a name can be used; lifetime is when the variable exists - Scope is about time; lifetime is about places in the file - Scope applies to functions; lifetime applies to variables > **Scope** is a property of the source code (which lines can use the name). **Lifetime** is a property of the running program. ? Can code in an outer block use a variable declared in an inner block? - Yes, as long as the inner block has already run - Yes, if the outer code uses the same type + No; inner blocks can see out, but outer blocks cannot see in > A name declared inside braces is only in scope until the closing brace. Code outside cannot use it. ? Why avoid `using namespace std;`? - It makes every program noticeably slower to run + It pulls in thousands of names that can clash with yours - It stops `std::cout` from working in that file - It is not allowed in modern C++ > It is legal, but it pulls every standard name into scope, which can clash with your names and cause confusing errors. ? What is shadowing? - Two functions with the same name in different files - A variable that is never used - Copying a variable into a function parameter + An inner variable hiding an outer one with the same name > The inner variable hides the outer one inside its block. It is legal, but easy to misread, so compilers can warn about it. ```
ideas:
1. Make two namespaces, `Metric` and `Imperial`, each with a function `double toBase(double)`. Call both from `main`.
2. Declare a variable inside a `for` loop's body and try to print it after the loop. Read the error.
3. Shadow a variable on purpose and predict what each print shows.

cards.q: What is the difference between scope and lifetime?
cards.a:
Scope is where a name can be used; lifetime is when the variable exists

**Scope** is a property of the source code (which lines can use the name). **Lifetime** is a property of the running program.

cards.q: Can code in an outer block use a variable declared in an inner block?
cards.a:
No; inner blocks can see out, but outer blocks cannot see in

A name declared inside braces is only in scope until the closing brace. Code outside cannot use it.

It pulls in thousands of names that can clash with yours

It is legal, but it pulls every standard name into scope, which can clash with your names and cause confusing errors.

An inner variable hiding an outer one with the same name

The inner variable hides the outer one inside its block. It is legal, but easy to misread, so compilers can warn about it.
